en: Udāna 2.2 Rājasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion, after their meal, as many bhikkhus as had returned from the alms round were sitting together in the assembly hall when this discussion arose among them:
“Friends, which of these two kings has greater wealth, more property, or a larger treasury?”
"Or one who is more victorious, or has greater mounts, or greater strength, or greater psychic power, or greater majesty—
such as King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or King Pasenadi of Kosala?
This was the conversation those bhikkhus were having when it was interrupted.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered and seated here now? And what was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished?"
“Here, Bhante, after we had returned from our almsround following our meal, while we were sitting gathered together in the assembly hall,
this discussion arose among us: ‘Friends, which of these two kings has greater wealth,
greater possessions, a greater treasury, a greater realm, greater vehicles, greater power, greater psychic potency, or greater majesty?’”
“Or was it King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or King Pasenadi of Kosala?
“This, Bhante, was our conversation that remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.
“Bhikkhus, it is not fitting for you—sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—to engage in such talk as this.”
“Bhikkhus, when you have gathered together, two things are to be practiced:
either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world,
and whatever heavenly bliss there is— these do not equal even a fraction of the happiness born of the destruction of craving.
“They are not worth a sixteenth part of it.
Second.
